theme: Miriam dies; the rock; the bronze serpent, look and live
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 20:1-21:35. This reading includes Moses’ great failure at Meribah, the death of Miriam and Aaron, and the story of the bronze serpent. Read slowly, and notice how one story leads into the next.
settingTheScene: Thirty-eight years have passed, and a new generation stands at Kadesh again. The first generation has largely died. Miriam dies, the people complain about water, and Moses and Aaron sin at the rock. Edom refuses passage. Aaron dies on Mount Hor. Then Israel complains again, and God sends fiery serpents, and then provides a way of healing. The chapters end with the first victories in Transjordan.
observation: Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh (20:1).
The people quarrel with Moses about water, saying, “Why have you brought the assembly of the LORD into this wilderness, that we should die here?” (20:3-5).
God says, “Take the staff… and tell the rock before their eyes to yield its water” (20:8).
Moses says, “Hear now, you rebels: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?” and strikes the rock twice (20:10-11).
God says, “Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land” (20:12).
Aaron dies on Mount Hor, and his garments are put on Eleazar (20:22-29).
The people speak against God and Moses: “We loathe this worthless food.” The LORD sends fiery serpents (21:4-6).
God says, “Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live” (21:8).
interpretation:
The sin of Moses at the rock is subtle, and it is easy to underestimate. God told him to speak to the rock. Instead, Moses struck it twice, and he said, “Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?” He took the credit that belonged to God. He struck instead of speaking, repeating an earlier command from Exodus 17. And he spoke in anger. The punishment seems severe, but leaders are held to a higher standard, and Moses had misrepresented God to the people. God had described himself as gracious, and Moses showed him as harsh.

The point is a sobering one: even Moses, the meekest man on earth, could fail. No human leader can bring the people into the promised land. The law cannot do it. Only another Joshua, only a greater leader, can.

The bronze serpent is among the strangest and most important stories in the Bible. The people have been bitten by snakes because of their sin. God does not remove the snakes. Instead, he gives a remedy that requires only a look. The cure is a serpent on a pole, the image of the very thing that is killing them. The ones who look live. There is no medicine, no effort, no payment. The simplest act of faith saves.

It is a story about how salvation works. The people had to believe that looking at a bronze snake would heal them. It is foolish by any natural reasoning. But God’s cure is often a matter of faith in his word, not an act of strength. “Everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.”

The progress from the death of Aaron to the lifting of the serpent to the first victories shows that God’s work continues even when leaders fail and die. The people move on toward the land, led by a God who does not die.
connection: Jesus said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14-15). The cross is the pole, and looking is believing. Paul says, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). 1 Corinthians 10:4 says that the rock was Christ, who was struck once and now gives living water freely (John 7:37-38).
application:
Think about what it means to “look and live.” Spend a few minutes looking to Christ on the cross.

Ask whether you have ever taken credit for something God did. Give it back.

Pray for leaders who have failed, and thank God that his work does not depend on any one person.
prayerPrompts: Look to Jesus lifted up, and tell him what you need healed.
Confess where you have taken credit that belongs to God.
Thank him that his work goes on despite our failure.
